warnings.action: Avoid St. John’s wort during pregnancy unless specialist-supervised.
warnings.alert_body: St John's Wort has been flagged for possible birth-defect risk and major drug interactions. If you are pregnant, talk to a specialist before any use.
warnings.detail: NCCIH notes potential increased birth-defect risk and major drug interaction potential.

warnings.action: Discuss St. John’s wort with the infant's clinician before use while breastfeeding, especially for a newborn or preterm infant.
warnings.alert_body: Limited breastfeeding reports describe infant colic, drowsiness, or lethargy. Discuss St. John’s wort with the infant's clinician before use, especially for a newborn or preterm infant.
warnings.alert_headline: Infant side effects have been reported
warnings.detail: Limited breastfeeding reports describe infant colic, drowsiness, or lethargy. LactMed prefers an alternative while nursing a newborn or preterm infant because published experience is limited.
warnings.informational_note: St. John’s wort has limited breastfeeding evidence and reported infant side effects.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / lactation

warnings.action: Avoid if taking calcium channel blockers or other CYP3A4-metabolized BP medications.
warnings.alert_body: St. John’s wort can induce drug-metabolizing enzymes and may reduce levels of some blood pressure medicines. If you take BP medication, review with your clinician before combining.
warnings.alert_headline: May reduce some BP medication levels
warnings.detail: St. John's Wort induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, reducing plasma levels of calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, amlodipine, verapamil) and potentially other antihypertensives.
warnings.informational_note: St John's Wort can affect blood pressure — relevant to people with high blood pressure.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / hypertension

warnings.action: Avoid combination. If SJW is discontinued, BP medications may suddenly become more potent, risking hypotension.
warnings.alert_body: St John's Wort speeds up drug metabolism via CYP3A4 and can lower levels of blood-pressure drugs. If you take antihypertensive medication, talk to your prescriber before use.
warnings.detail: Potent CYP3A4/P-gp induction reduces plasma levels of calcium channel blockers and other CYP3A4-metabolized antihypertensives, compromising BP control.
warnings.informational_note: St John's Wort induces CYP3A4 — relevant to people on antihypertensive medications.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / antihypertensives

warnings.action: Do not combine St. John's Wort with warfarin or other vitamin-K antagonists. Discuss alternatives with your prescriber.
warnings.alert_body: St John’s wort can reduce warfarin’s anticoagulant effect. Tell your anticoagulant prescriber about any use or change and ask about INR monitoring.
warnings.detail: St John’s wort can induce drug metabolism and reduce warfarin anticoagulation. S-warfarin is predominantly metabolized by CYP2C9, while other pathways contribute to R-warfarin; primary work found increased clearance of both enantiomers.
warnings.informational_note: St. John's Wort is a strong CYP3A4 inducer — relevant to anyone on warfarin or many other prescription drugs.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / anticoagulants

warnings.action: Do not combine St. John's Wort with transplant immunosuppressants.
warnings.alert_body: If you take immunosuppressants, do not combine with this product. St. John's Wort speeds up the breakdown of tacrolimus and cyclosporine. This can cause transplant rejection.
warnings.alert_headline: Do not combine with transplant drugs
warnings.detail: CYP3A4 induction (opposite mechanism to grapefruit) → reduced exposure to tacrolimus, cyclosporine → therapy failure and transplant rejection.
warnings.informational_note: St. John's Wort is a strong CYP3A4 inducer — opposite mechanism to grapefruit (drug failure, not toxicity).
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / immunosuppressants

warnings.action: Avoid with CYP3A4-metabolized statins or monitor lipid levels closely.
warnings.alert_body: St John’s wort can reduce the effect of some statins. Talk to your statin prescriber before use; the effect differs by drug and preparation.
warnings.detail: St John’s wort can reduce exposure or lipid-lowering effect of susceptible statins. A simvastatin study found reduced AUC while pravastatin was unchanged, and an atorvastatin study measured increased LDL; reduced drug effect should not be described as increased statin muscle or liver toxicity.
warnings.informational_note: St John's Wort affects statin pathways — relevant to people on statin therapy.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / statins

warnings.action: Avoid unsupervised combination with sedatives or antidepressants.
warnings.alert_body: St John’s wort can reduce exposure to some sedatives, including alprazolam. Ask your prescriber about the specific medicine before use.
warnings.detail: A human study found about half the alprazolam AUC and doubled clearance after St John’s wort. This induction finding should not be described as increased sedation from higher benzodiazepine exposure.
warnings.informational_note: St John's Wort has sedative activity — relevant to people on sedatives or sleep medications.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / sedatives

warnings.action: Do not combine St John’s wort with serotonergic antidepressants without specialist guidance. Do not stop prescribed treatment to use it; the prescriber must determine any medication change or product-specific washout.
warnings.alert_body: St John's Wort raises serotonin activity. If you take an SSRI or SNRI antidepressant, do not combine — the combination can cause serotonin syndrome.
warnings.alert_headline: Do not combine with SSRIs or SNRIs
warnings.detail: St John's Wort increases serotonin levels via monoamine reuptake inhibition. Combined with SSRIs/SNRIs, this causes additive serotonergic stimulation leading to serotonin syndrome — a potentially fatal toxidrome (hyperthermia, clonus, agitation, seizures). Multiple case reports and pharmacovigilance alerts.
warnings.informational_note: St John's Wort raises serotonin — relevant to people on SSRI or SNRI antidepressants.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / antidepressants_ssri_snri

warnings.action: Avoid unsupervised combination. The prescribing clinician must manage any medication change and product-specific washout.
warnings.alert_body: Do not combine St John’s wort with an MAOI without specialist review. Do not stop or change your prescription to use the supplement.
warnings.detail: A serious interaction precaution applies when St John’s wort is combined with MAOIs. The retained NCCIH content does not establish the detailed hypericin MAO-A mechanism or a universal washout interval.
warnings.informational_note: St. John's Wort has serotonergic and MAO-A activity — relevant to anyone on MAOIs.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / maois

warnings.action: Do not rely on oral contraceptives while using St. John's Wort. Use additional non-hormonal contraception or discontinue St. John's Wort.
warnings.alert_body: If you take oral contraceptives, do not combine with this product. St. John's Wort lowers the level of birth-control pills in your blood and can lead to unintended pregnancy.
warnings.detail: CYP3A4 induction reduces ethinyl estradiol exposure → contraception failure and breakthrough bleeding documented in clinical literature.
warnings.informational_note: St. John's Wort reduces oral contraceptive efficacy.
warnings.title: St. John's Wort Herb Extract / oral_contraceptives

warnings.action: If you take a CYP2D6-substrate prescription drug at high-dose St. John's Wort (≥900 mg/day), your prescriber may want to monitor for changes in drug effect. The CYP3A4 interaction at any dose is the dominant clinical concern — see the existing contraindication.
warnings.alert_body: The CYP2D6 effect of St John’s wort is uncertain and preparation-dependent. Tell your prescriber about use and review your specific medicines.
warnings.detail: Human probe studies did not establish a significant CYP2D6 effect under their tested regimens. This does not prove every St John’s wort preparation is interaction-free, but it does not support a proven 900 mg CYP2D6 threshold.
warnings.informational_note: SJW at ≥900 mg/day has mixed-direction CYP2D6 effect — distinct from its dominant CYP3A4 induction.

ingredients.name: Magnesium
ingredients.notes: Schuette 1994 (PMID:7815675) compared 100 mg isotope-labeled magnesium diglycinate with oxide in 12 ileal-resection patients. Overall absorption did not differ (23.5% versus 22.8%); a four-patient subgroup with poor oxide absorption benefited and diglycinate was better tolerated. This does not establish superiority or inferiority versus citrate in healthy adults. Walker 2003 (PMID:14596323) tested an amino-acid chelate; its abstract does not identify that preparation as exact glycinate. Sean’s 2026-10-13 calibration retains bio_score 12 with moderate evidence; tolerability and absorption are distinct outcomes. Buffered bisglycinate and lysinate/glycinate preparations are not aliases for this exact glycine-chelate form. Unresolved named preparations retain the existing disclosed-form-unmapped assessment hold; generic amino-acid chelate has its own owner. EFSA 2018 opinion 10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5292 also reports an unpublished 14-volunteer healthy-adult crossover comparing bisglycinate, buffered bisglycinate, dimagnesium malate and oxide. These are distinct preparations; this dossier does not justify treating every buffered or mixed-ligand product as plain glycinate.

ingredients.notes: Schuette 1994 (PMID:7815675) compared 100 mg isotope-labeled magnesium diglycinate with oxide in 12 ileal-resection patients. Overall absorption did not differ (23.5% versus 22.8%); a four-patient subgroup with poor oxide absorption benefited and diglycinate was better tolerated. This does not establish superiority or inferiority versus citrate in healthy adults. Walker 2003 (PMID:14596323) tested an amino-acid chelate; its abstract does not identify that preparation as exact glycinate. Sean’s 2026-10-13 calibration retains bio_score 12 with moderate evidence; tolerability and absorption are distinct outcomes. Buffered bisglycinate and lysinate/glycinate preparations are not aliases for this exact glycine-chelate form. Unresolved named preparations retain the existing disclosed-form-unmapped assessment hold; generic amino-acid chelate has its own owner. EFSA 2018 opinion 10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5292 also reports an unpublished 14-volunteer healthy-adult crossover comparing bisglycinate, buffered bisglycinate, dimagnesium malate and oxide. These are distinct preparations; this dossier does not justify treating every buffered or mixed-ligand product as plain glycinate.

A separate systematic review of prolonged use in healthy adults found effects only under specific conditions and raised unresolved long-term TMAO questions.
